Visual inspection of central tendencies is not reliable
Given any set of collected data, there will almost always be some variation
Differences between data sets may be due to just normal variation!
Two sets of ten tosses with different but fair dice
– First dice gives
6, 2, 4, 4, 2, 6, 4, 2, 5, 6 (M = 4.1)
– Second dice gives
6, 4, 4, 5, 4, 4, 2, 1, 4, 5 (M = 3.9)
If they are both fair dice, shouldn’t their outputs have the same probability? 
Does this mean that the dice are not fair? Given any set of data (even dice 
throws), there will always be some variation
The question is whether this variation is explainable by normal variation
(Do you believe that the world is fixed and stable or that everything
moves and changes?)
Is a difference of 0.2 explainable? Is the average stable enough? What about 
1000 attempts?

Signal versus noise
Given two datasets, the difference between their means is the “signal”
The change that we think that we introduced into the dataset by manipulating 
the independent variables
The variability is the “noise” that is introduced by random factors beyond our control
Given any dataset, there will always be some “noise,” so we cannot trust that 
the “signal” tells the story 100%
The question is: How much noise can we expect to encounter in a normal situation?
Meaning: When can we trust that the difference that we’re seeing is a reliable 
difference, and not just because of noise?

The role of the normal distribution in a t-test
The normal distribution allows the t-test to say something about how likely it is that 
the differences between the means of the two groups are systematic, or just 
happened by matter of chance
Default is the Null (H0) = observed differences are chance occurrences
Given enough data, or a small enough variability, we can reject the Null in favor 
of the Alternative (HA or H1) if:
– There is probably a systematic difference between the means, and
– I am so-and-so much confident in my decision (e.g., 95% convinced)
If the t-test shows that the difference between the means (the signal) is more 
than what would be expected purely by chance,
– then we say that the difference is statistically significant
– Certain researchers would then reject H0 and accept H1
Be aware that the ‘frequentist approach’ illustrated here can only reject the Null or 
fail to do so; it cannot demonstrate the Alternative. Moreover, detecting no notable 
difference does not say that there is no difference. It also does not say that the two 
samples were drawn from the same population!

If the t-test shows that the difference between the means (the signal) is more than 
what would be expected purely by chance, then we say that the difference is 
statistically significant. How does the t-test “show” us this with a value?
The numerator of the t-value is the difference between the means of the groups
The denominator is the variability of the groups
Intuitively, the larger the t-value is, the more significant the difference (or the signal) is, 
compared to the noise
Significance depends on the size of the dataset (the degrees of freedom)
(i.e., the number of scores that are free to vary, see next slide)
And on the risk level (or alpha level or rejection area) that we set: = .05
– Gives the level of confidence we want to have before making a judgement
– Usually set at 95% (or a 5% chance that we might be wrong): p < .05
– But that is pretty arbitrary and depends on the situation
(10% patients cured may not be ‘significant’ but may save thousands of lives)

Step-by-step click paths to access the General Linear Model (GLM) in SPSS
1. Open SPSS: Start SPSS and open your dataset
2. Analyze Menu: Click on the Analyze menu at the top of the SPSS window
3. General Linear Model: Hover over General Linear Model in the drop-down menu. This will expand to show more options
4. Choose the Type of GLM:
Univariate: For a single dependent variable
Multivariate: For multiple dependent variables
Repeated Measures: For repeated measures data
Variance Components: For variance components analysis
More detailed path for each type:
Univariate GLM:
1. Analyze > General Linear Model > Univariate...
2. In the dialog box that appears, specify your dependent variable and fixed factors (independent variables)
Multivariate GLM:
1. Analyze > General Linear Model > Multivariate...
2. In the dialog box that appears, specify your dependent variables and fixed factors
Repeated Measures GLM:
1. Analyze > General Linear Model > Repeated Measures...
2. Define your within-subject factor(s) and then click Define to specify the dependent variables and other factors
Variance Components:
1. Analyze > General Linear Model > Variance Components...
2. Specify your model in the dialog box that appears
Example for Univariate GLM:
1. Analyze > General Linear Model > Univariate...
2. In the "Univariate" dialog box:
Move your dependent variable to the Dependent Variable box
Move your independent variables to the Fixed Factor(s) box
Optionally, you can add covariates by moving them to the Covariate(s) box
3. Click on Model to specify the model if needed
4. Click on Options to select additional statistics or plots
5. Click OK to run the analysis
This will run the GLM analysis and provide you with the output, including tables and charts, based on your specifications

users (e.g., AutoCAD or OmniGraffle), and the tasks 
involve extremely frequent menu selections, then

During the pandemic, a student of Media Entertainment investigated 
the effect of two types of VR helmets on body temperature. The VR 
was supposed to counter boredom but wearing it should not be at 
the cost of increasing the user’s face temperature 
For her measurements, the student used several Heaco MDI908 
medical non-contact infrared thermometers, which she calibrated 
against one another, finding for all devices systematically 
temperatures of 37.0 Cwith a standard deviation of around 0.5 C
The student sampled 220 participants, 110 for each VR helmet, with a 
G*power of about 80% to 90% of correctly rejecting the Null
Luckily and as expected, using different infrared thermometers did 
not yield a significant effect. In addition, two-group independent 
samples t-test also showed no significant effect for VR headset: t(219) = 
-.05, p = .896, showing that VR helmet 1 (MVRh1 = 36.9, SD = .20) nor 
VR helmet 2 (MVRh2 = 37.0, SD = .10) made a significant impact on 
the users’ facial temperature
The student concluded that both helmets are safe to use, not causing 
any extra inconvenience during those already stressful times
Does anyone have a 
problem with that 
conclusion?
